lesson_title: Three Ways to Push Air Up a Hill: How Rain Happens
hook_text: Every raindrop that ever fell needed one thing: something to shove the air upwards.
clip_script: Every drop of rain that has ever fallen came from the same four steps. Air goes up. Air cools. Air fills up. Water falls out. Only ONE thing changes between the three rainfall types: what pushed the air up. Push number one — the mountain. Wet air comes in off the sea, meets a mountain, has nowhere to go but up. It rains on the side facing the wind, then comes down the far side warm and dry. That is why the eastern Drakensberg is green and the Little Karoo behind the Cape mountains is ostrich country. Push number two — the hot ground. January in Gauteng: the ground bakes, air shoots upward like smoke off a fire, towers all day, and at four o'clock the sky opens. Short, violent, loud, sometimes hail, often over your street while the next suburb stays dry. Push number three — the cold bulldozer. Cold air marches in from the south-west, and because it is heavier it shoves under the warm air and lifts it clean off the ground. That is Cape Town's entire winter. Mountain. Hot ground. Bulldozer. Never confuse them again.
visual_style: Three quick side-on cross-sections drawn in bold lines — air riding a mountain, air boiling off a hot plain, a wedge of blue shoving orange air upward — each with a South African place name stamping in.
pacing: Fast common opening, then three equal hard-hitting beats, ending on the three-word list.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to name any cloud in the sky from four Latin words.
